title: Breathless on awake VA ECMO
subtitle: A 41-year-old woman with fulminant myocarditis, extubated yesterday for mobilization, now tachypneic with an alkalemic radial gas.
objectives: Explain why a spontaneously breathing patient on peripheral VA ECMO can have a hypocapnic right radial gas while the brain is hypercapnic.
Trace the iatrogenic loop in which reducing sweep in response to a low right radial PaCO2 drives further tachypnea.
State which sampling sites answer the oxygenation question and which answer the decarboxylation question on peripheral VA ECMO, and why they differ.
Build a plan for tachypnea on awake VA ECMO that separates the respiratory-drive problem from the circuit problem.
Contrast East-West (differential hypocapnia) with North-South (differential hypoxemia) and name the single right radial finding that separates them.

stages.title: Presentation
stages.narrative:
A 41-year-old woman with fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis is on day 5 of peripheral femoro-femoral VA ECMO. Her native cardiac function is recovering slowly, with the aortic valve opening on most beats and a modestly pulsatile arterial trace. She was extubated yesterday to allow early mobilization and physiotherapy.

She has a right radial arterial line. The ECMO flow is moderate and the sweep has been stable for three days. Her ventilation is spontaneous on nasal cannula. Yesterday evening's right radial gas was unremarkable: normal pH, normal PaCO2, and a PaO2 appropriate for the oxygen she was breathing. [REVIEW]

This morning she is restless and the nurse reports a respiratory rate in the high 20s, up from the mid-teens overnight. She says she feels short of breath. The physiotherapist had her sitting on the edge of the bed an hour earlier. [REVIEW]

Right radial ABG now, on 2 L nasal cannula: pH 7.52, PaCO2 29 mmHg, PaO2 94 mmHg. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Give your differential for the tachypnea, say what the right radial gas does and does not tell you, and commit to what you would do with the sweep gas right now.
questions.modelAnswer:
The differential for tachypnea on awake VA ECMO is ordinary and should be worked through in the ordinary way: pain, anxiety, delirium, exertion from physiotherapy, aspiration, evolving pneumonia, pulmonary edema from inadequate unloading, pulmonary embolism, metabolic acidosis, and the circuit itself (hemolysis, oxygenator dysfunction).

What the right radial gas tells you: the blood reaching the right arm, and therefore the brachiocephalic territory, is alkalemic and hypocapnic with a PaO2 that is entirely normal for 2 L of oxygen. That normal PaO2 is itself informative: the lungs are oxygenating the blood they receive, so this is not a lung-failure picture. In an awake patient breathing at 28 per minute, a low right radial PaCO2 is exactly what native lungs that are being hyperventilated would produce. It does not tell you whether the brain as a whole is hypocapnic, because on peripheral VA ECMO the brain is not supplied by one circulation.

What it does not tell you: anything about the carbon dioxide content of the retrograde ECMO blood that is reaching the left common carotid and the descending aorta. For that you need a post-oxygenator gas, a left radial gas, or a central venous or mixed venous PCO2.

Whatever you decided about the sweep, notice that you decided it with one of the two circulations unmeasured.

stages.title: New data
stages.narrative:
The overnight team interpreted the morning gas as respiratory alkalosis from excessive CO2 clearance and reduced the sweep gas flow in two steps over four hours. The respiratory rate is now in the mid-30s. She is now visibly distressed, diaphoretic, and intermittently confused. [REVIEW]

Right radial ABG on 2 L nasal cannula: pH 7.56, PaCO2 25 mmHg, PaO2 97 mmHg. [REVIEW]

A post-oxygenator gas is drawn for the first time since extubation: PaCO2 61 mmHg, pH 7.24. [REVIEW]

ECMO flow is unchanged. Echo shows the aortic valve opening with each beat and the LV ejecting modestly. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Explain, step by step, how the right radial PaCO2 fell while the post-oxygenator PaCO2 rose, and why the patient is breathing faster despite an alkalemic radial gas. Then say why this has been called East-West.
questions.modelAnswer:
This is the sequence Rosenberg, Thakuria, and Vandenbriele describe in their 2025 Circulation paper, which named the phenomenon. [REVIEW]

1. An awake patient on peripheral VA ECMO develops mild tachypnea for an ordinary reason: exertion, pain, anxiety, early sepsis.
2. Higher minute ventilation clears more CO2 through the native lungs. The hypocapnic blood the LV ejects reaches the brachiocephalic trunk first. The right radial line samples it and reads low PaCO2, high pH.
3. The clinician reads that as global hypocapnia and reduces the sweep gas to clear less CO2 through the circuit.
4. The retrograde ECMO blood arriving at the arch is now hypercapnic. It enters the cerebral circulation through the left common carotid (and, depending on where the mixing zone sits, the left subclavian and vertebral territory) and reaches the respiratory centers.
5. Hypercapnic blood at the chemoreceptors drives a further rise in respiratory rate and minute ventilation. The native lungs clear even more CO2, so the right radial PaCO2 falls further, which looks like the sweep is still too high.
6. The team reduces the sweep again. Each cycle makes the ECMO blood more hypercapnic and the right radial gas more hypocapnic. The result is respiratory exhaustion, worsening cerebral hypercapnia with its effects on cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure, and often reintubation for a presumed primary pulmonary problem.

Why East-West: the authors chose the name by analogy with North-South syndrome. In North-South the mismatch is between upper body and lower body (oxygen). Here the mismatch is lateral, between the brachiocephalic territory on the right, which sees native lung blood, and the left carotid territory, which sees ECMO blood. The right side of the brain and the right arm are hypocapnic. The left side of the brain is hypercapnic. The name is a mnemonic for the anatomy, and the acronym RIDDLER (Relatively Increased CO2 Delivered to the brain from the Descending aorta Leading to an Elevated Respiratory rate) is the mechanism. [REVIEW]

stages.title: Decision point
stages.narrative: The attending has been called. The patient is tiring. The nurse asks whether to prepare for reintubation. The perfusionist asks what to do with the sweep. ECMO flow and circuit pressures are unchanged. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Commit to a plan for the next hour. Say what you do with the sweep, what you sample and how often, how you decide about reintubation, and what you tell the overnight team to do differently next time.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Sweep.** Restore it, then titrate upward against the post-oxygenator (or left radial) PaCO2 and pH, not the right radial. Rosenberg and colleagues suggest matching sweep to blood flow at a 1:1 ratio as a starting point in the maintenance phase and targeting physiologically normal pH and PCO2 in the post-oxygenator or left radial sample. [REVIEW] That is expert opinion from one group, not a guideline, and the right number for this patient is the one that normalizes the ECMO-side gas. As the ECMO blood reaching the chemoreceptors becomes normocapnic the drive to hyperventilate should fall, and the right radial PaCO2 should rise toward normal on its own.

**Sampling.** Paired gases: right radial and post-oxygenator, drawn together, repeated after each sweep change and then at an interval the team agrees. A left radial line is a reasonable addition if the team wants a continuous arterial trace of ECMO-side blood. A central venous or mixed venous PCO2 adds information about global CO2 kinetics. Rosenberg and colleagues list all three. [REVIEW] End-tidal CO2 is unhelpful here: it reflects native lung CO2 and will track the right radial, which is the misleading number.

**Reintubation.** The decision rests on work of breathing, mental status, and trajectory, not on the radial gas. If the sweep correction produces a clear fall in respiratory rate and the patient settles within an hour, the loop has been broken and she stays extubated. Nasal high-flow or noninvasive ventilation can reduce work of breathing while the gases equilibrate. If she continues to tire, is increasingly confused, or develops concurrent differential hypoxemia (the right radial PaO2 has been normal throughout, which is one reason this is not a primary lung problem), then sedation, intubation, and if necessary neuromuscular blockade are the right call, and the authors say so. Reintubation is a failure of recognition, not a failure of the decision to reintubate. [REVIEW]

**Treat the trigger.** Whatever started the tachypnea still needs addressing: analgesia, anxiolysis, a look for sepsis or aspiration, and an echo to confirm the LV is not distending so that pulmonary edema is not the driver.

**What to tell the overnight team.** On an awake peripheral VA ECMO patient, the right radial gas answers the oxygen question (it is the earliest site to fall if the lungs are failing, and it is the pessimist). It does not answer the CO2 question in a hyperventilating patient (it is the optimist, because the lungs are over-clearing). Never adjust the sweep on a right radial PaCO2 without a post-oxygenator gas drawn at the same time. That rule can be written into the unit's awake ECMO guidance. [NMH protocol, insert]

stages.title: The morning after
stages.narrative:
The sweep was restored and titrated to the post-oxygenator gas. Her respiratory rate settled into the high teens within two hours and she slept. This morning she is lucid, comfortable on 2 L nasal cannula, with paired gases that agree: right radial PaCO2 38, post-oxygenator PaCO2 40, PaO2 appropriate for the oxygen she is breathing. [REVIEW]

The physiotherapist is back and wants to get her to the chair. The day-team fellow is unsure whether yesterday's episode means mobilization should stop. The attending asks you two things: what the plan is for today's session, and, as a thought experiment, how the same right radial line would have behaved if her lungs rather than her respiratory drive had been the problem.

questions.prompt: Should she mobilize today? If yes, what changes about how the session is run and monitored so that yesterday does not repeat?
questions.modelAnswer:
Yes. The episode was iatrogenic, not a contraindication to the awake strategy. The trigger (exertion with physiotherapy) is predictable and recurs every day she mobilizes, so the plan should anticipate it rather than react to it. [REVIEW]

- **Paired gases around the session.** Right radial and post-oxygenator drawn together before, during if she becomes tachypneic, and after. The post-oxygenator number is the one that governs sweep. The right radial number is expected to fall during exertion and that is not an indication to touch the sweep.
- **Pre-agreed sweep plan.** The bedside team should know before the session what the sweep will be, what post-oxygenator target it is titrated to, and that no change is made on a right radial gas alone. Writing this into the awake ECMO order set removes the 3 a.m. reasoning. [NMH protocol, insert]
- **Treat the drive, not the number.** Analgesia and anxiolysis before the session if either was a contributor. A respiratory rate in the high 20s during exertion is acceptable if she is comfortable and the post-oxygenator gas is normocapnic. A rate that keeps climbing after rest is the signal to stop and sample.
- **ECMO flow.** Leave it. Yesterday's problem was not flow, and changing several things at once destroys the ability to interpret the next gas.
- **Handoff.** The overnight note should say explicitly that a hypocapnic right radial gas in this patient is expected with exertion and is managed by sampling the post-oxygenator gas, not by lowering sweep.

The larger point for the fellow: awake peripheral VA ECMO shifts the monitoring burden from the ventilator to the clinician's understanding of where each sample comes from. That is the price of the strategy and the reason it belongs in units that have thought it through. [REVIEW]

questions.prompt: Thought experiment: same cannulation, same line, but suppose her lungs had failed overnight instead of her respiratory drive rising. Describe how the right radial gas would have looked, what the post-oxygenator gas would have shown, and why the two scenarios demand opposite responses from the same sampling site.
questions.modelAnswer:
If the lungs had failed, the right radial PaO2 would have fallen below what the inspired oxygen should produce, because the brachiocephalic trunk is supplied by native ejection and native ejection carries lung-conditioned blood. The right radial PaCO2 would have been normal or high, not low, because failing lungs do not over-clear CO2 even when the patient is tachypneic. The post-oxygenator gas would have been normal, because the circuit was never the problem. The left foot would have been pink. That is North-South syndrome, differential hypoxemia, covered in its own case in this library. [REVIEW]

Set the two side by side on the one line that matters:

- **East-West (yesterday).** Right radial: PaO2 normal for FiO2, PaCO2 low. Post-oxygenator: PaCO2 high after the sweep was cut. The circuit side is where the abnormality lives. Response: fix the sweep, leave the lungs alone.
- **North-South (the counterfactual).** Right radial: PaO2 low for FiO2, PaCO2 normal or high. Post-oxygenator: normal. The native side is where the abnormality lives. Response: fix or bypass the lungs (optimize ventilation, VAV, proximal arterial return), leave the sweep alone.

The right radial is the earliest true alarm for the oxygen problem and a false alarm for the CO2 problem in a breathing patient. The same anatomy produces both behaviors. A fellow who knows only North-South will cut the sweep on yesterday's gas. A fellow who knows only East-West will dismiss a genuinely falling PaO2 as another radial artifact. The discriminator is the PaO2 relative to the inspired oxygen, read together with the post-oxygenator gas. Neither syndrome can be diagnosed from the right radial alone. [REVIEW]

The two can coexist, but only if the lungs are actually injured. In this patient they were not, which is exactly why the PaO2 stayed normal throughout and why the hypocapnia should have been read as hyperventilation from the first gas.

teachingPoints:
- On peripheral VA ECMO the brain is supplied by two circulations. The right radial samples the native one. The left carotid territory, and often the vertebrobasilar territory, sees ECMO blood.
- In a spontaneously breathing patient, a low right radial PaCO2 reflects native lung hyperventilation, not circuit over-clearance. Reducing sweep in response delivers hypercapnic ECMO blood to the chemoreceptors and drives further tachypnea. This loop is RIDDLER or East-West syndrome.
- Titrate decarboxylation to the post-oxygenator or left radial gas. The right radial answers the oxygen question, not the CO2 question, when the patient is breathing.
- Paired sampling (right radial plus post-oxygenator, drawn together) is the habit that prevents the loop.
- End-tidal CO2 tracks the native lungs and is misleading in this setting.
- East-West and North-South share anatomy but point in opposite directions. The discriminator on the right radial is the PaO2 relative to inspired oxygen: normal in East-West, low in North-South. Read it with a post-oxygenator gas every time.
- The syndrome is newly named and incompletely characterized. Its frequency, the CO2 gradient that produces symptoms, and the best monitoring strategy are not established.
pitfalls:
- Treating a hypocapnic right radial gas in an awake VA ECMO patient as a sweep problem without a post-oxygenator sample.
- Diagnosing primary pulmonary deterioration or aspiration pneumonitis in a tachypneic awake ECMO patient without first excluding iatrogenic cerebral hypercapnia.
- Using end-tidal CO2 to guide sweep.
- Assuming the mixing zone is fixed. It moves with native contractility, ECMO flow, and vascular tone.
- Learning only one of the two differential syndromes and applying its logic to the other. The PaO2 relative to inspired oxygen separates them.
- Forgetting that reintubation, once the loop has run for hours, may be unavoidable and is not a reason to abandon the awake strategy in the next patient.
controversies:
**Nomenclature and reality.** East-West and RIDDLER were coined in a single 2025 Circulation Frame of Reference article, with a subsequent AACN teaching session in 2026. There is no case series, no incidence estimate, and no agreed definition. Some clinicians regard it as a labeled restatement of a known risk of awake peripheral VA ECMO rather than a new syndrome. Others see the naming as useful precisely because the loop is counterintuitive and the label makes it teachable. Both views are defensible. [REVIEW]

**Whether the lateral framing is accurate.** The name implies right-left asymmetry via brachiocephalic versus left carotid supply. The respiratory centers are brainstem structures supplied largely by the vertebrobasilar system, which draws from both subclavians, so the relevant question may be less about the left carotid than about the watershed relative to the subclavian origins. The physiology of the loop does not depend on which arch branch carries the hypercapnic blood, only that some of the brain's supply does. Faculty should decide how precisely to present the anatomy. [REVIEW]

**The 1:1 sweep-to-flow starting point.** This is one group's suggestion, not a validated target. Many centers titrate sweep purely to a chosen gas target without a flow ratio. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Awake VA ECMO itself.** The strategy is supported by observational data (Montero and colleagues) and by the general case against prolonged sedation and ventilation, but it has not been tested against a conventional strategy in a trial. Which patients, on which configurations, with which monitoring, remains center practice. [NMH protocol, insert]

**Monitoring.** Whether every awake peripheral VA ECMO patient should have a left radial line in addition to the right radial, or whether intermittent post-oxygenator sampling is sufficient, is unsettled and partly a question of resources and line-related risk. [REVIEW]
discussWithAttending: You have a right radial line and a post-oxygenator port. Argue for and against adding a left radial line in every awake peripheral VA ECMO patient. What would change your mind?

The paper suggests 1:1 sweep to flow as a starting point. Reconstruct from first principles what determines the right sweep in a patient with partial native lung function, and say whether a ratio makes sense at all.

This morning's team reduced the sweep in response to a gas. That is a reasonable action in a sedated, ventilated VA ECMO patient. What exactly about extubation changes the interpretation of the same number?
Design the paired-gas and sweep plan you would want written into an awake VA ECMO protocol around physiotherapy sessions, so that the overnight team does not have to reason this out at 3 a.m.
Is the awake strategy worth these risks in a patient whose native heart is only beginning to recover? Defend the decision to extubate on day 4, then make the case for waiting.

reviewChecklist: Framing: the case follows the Circulation paper's mechanism (differential decarboxylation driven by native hyperventilation and an iatrogenic sweep reduction). Your initial description emphasized lateral flow variation between brachiocephalic and left carotid. The case uses that anatomy as the substrate and the loop as the mechanism. Confirm this is the framing you want, and edit the 'Why East-West' passage in Stage 2 if not.

All gas values are synthetic and set per Dr. Giguere's direction: right radial PaO2 normal for the inspired oxygen throughout the East-West phase (94 then 97 mmHg on 2 L), PaCO2 in the 25 to 30 range (29 then 25), respiratory rate high 20s rising to mid-30s, post-oxygenator PaCO2 61 and pH 7.24. The PaO2 stays normal throughout. Morning-after paired gases (right radial PaCO2 38, post-oxygenator 40) are synthetic. Confirm they are the illustrative numbers you want.

Stage 1 vignette: Impella removed at Dr. Giguere's direction (2026-10-27) so the mixing cloud between the brachiocephalic trunk and left subclavian reflects native ejection alone. Extubation on day 4 for mobilization stated as unit practice.
Stage 3 model answer: the 1:1 sweep-to-flow starting point is attributed to Rosenberg 2025 and labeled expert opinion. Confirm you want it included at all, and insert NMH's sweep titration practice.
Stage 3 model answer: the statement that end-tidal CO2 is unhelpful here is my reasoning, not from the paper. Confirm or delete.

Stage 4 is now the recovery day: paired gases, a mobilization plan, and a counterfactual contrast with North-South posed as a thought experiment. The earlier draft introduced aspiration to force the contrast and was removed at Dr. Giguere's direction because her lungs are normal throughout. Confirm the mobilization plan matches NMH awake ECMO practice.

Controversies: the vertebrobasilar point (respiratory centers supplied via subclavians rather than the left carotid) is my anatomical observation, not from any cited source. Decide whether to keep, soften, or remove it.

Controversies: the characterization of the syndrome as newly named, single-source, and without a series is accurate as of October 2026 to my knowledge. Re-check the literature before release in case a series has since appeared.
